Welcome
We’re glad you’re here
Welcome to OURS

Tonight we gather around one crucial conviction: the future is something we make happen, not something that we let happen to us. We can imagine, discover, and build the world we want to live in. Everyone in this room, on these walls, and on the mic is here because they're already doing exactly that: turning a vision of what's possible into concrete reality.

Take in the gallery, test your governance skills in Systems of Power, relax and become inspired by Visions of the Future. But most importantly:

talk to someone. Talk to everyone. The reason we’re gathered in person is to experience this together, make connections, form collaborations, and learn things from each other that will catalyze our own journey ahead.

After all, the future is OURS.

Provocateurs
Erika Alden DeBenedictis
Physicist & biological engineer
CEO, Pioneer Labs
Erika is a physicist and biological engineer interested in solving big problems using evolution. She studied at Caltech (undergrad, computer science) and MIT (grad school, biological engineering). She led an academic lab at the Francis Crick Institute in London, where she invented robotics accelerated evolution methods. She is now the founder and CEO of Pioneer Labs, a Focused Research Organization (FRO) engineering life to make Mars more habitable.

OURS Salon & Exhibition 2026
Geoff Anders
Philosopher
Founder, Leverage
Geoff Anders is a philosopher and backer of revolutionary science. He is the founder of Leverage (leverage.institute) and has co-founded, advised, and supported nearly a dozen organizations as part of his work. He believes that the path to a better future will involve many surprises. Glimpses of the future are everywhere, but it takes great work to fully humanize them and bring them into the present.
7
Visions of the Future
Installation
Visions of the Future
The future is imagined, argued for, competed over, collaborated on, and ultimately built. Everyone who contributes begins from their own vantage point. The more of reality we come to understand, and the more of one another’s perspectives we take in, the more of the future we can see. That is part of what this installation is for.
Across these screens, various visionaries are thinking and speaking on their contributions to tomorrow. People from many disciplines and fields answer the same question: what tomorrow are you working to make real? Maybe it’s a world with geothermal cities, or without death, or where we’ve figured out mental preservation during long space voyages. These are not predictions, and they are not wishes. They are commitments, spoken aloud by people already acting on them.
This is what shaping the future actually looks like: many people, working on many hard problems, each from where they stand, together. Now add your voice. Find the tomorrow you are willing to work for, and go make it real. The future belongs to the people who show up to build it, and there is room, and need, for you.

Gallery
From Olli Payne, Director, FFA
Curatorial Statement
I am a futurist. It’s a simple fact. Maybe it’s a label, but more than that, it’s something that I can feel phenomenologically, in my bones and my tendons and behind my eyes; the will to see, the drive to act, toward the future.
When I was young I adored Ray Bradbury’s work, and in awe of the worlds he built using advanced technology. The characters were privileged to live in realities that had solved so many of humanity’s problems, yet there were always more plaguing them. I would sit and write out what further technological innovations could be introduced to save them, these vexingly and unavoidably troubled ghosts on the pages.
Over time, I have come to understand that while there is much value in advances in software and hard tech, the bottleneck is actually social technology. The quagmires of Bradbury’s characters were rooted in culture. Burning books didn’t result from installing screens into walls, it emerged from demand for complacency over thinking, feeling, or acting. This kind of social decay, to my horror, can be seen in the cautionary science fiction tale but is also taking root in the world around us.
I believe art to be a sacred cure – it can inform, inspire, ignite, and compel us. It shatters complacency and reminds us of what we find beautiful and good and shows us that it is achievable. It’s the expression and the reception, made tangible materially and transferable socially and spiritually. For these reasons, the art that’s upstream of our culture’s idea of the future will shape our future.
The collection of works presented in this exhibit is the result of my search for that cure in the creations of others. It’s the manifestation of my attempt to gather and show proof that we can make a conscious choice about the future we pursue, from vision to realization. Thank you for being here to experience that.

Gallery
Featured Artist
RERO · A New City Will Be Built…
Burnt wood & metal
67×49 in

RERO’s work is built upon a unique visual grammar: the use of the Verdana font (a symbol of the digital era), systematically crossed out with a horizontal line. Driven by punchlines and aphorisms, the betrayal of images, and semantic wordplay, RERO’s work lies at the crossroads of urban practices, land art, and conceptual gestures.

The dark, textured medium of burnt wood materializes the end of a model: that of rigid structures inherited from a saturated present. Yet, it is from the debris of this old world consumed by fire that the light of the letters emerges. By ending his phrase with an ellipsis, the artist refuses to close the narrative. The strikethrough creates a salutary void: it opens a breach and a space of indeterminacy, directly inviting visitors to reclaim their agency to collectively reimagine the contours of tomorrow's city.

“In Rero's work, art is an alarm system attempting to awaken the atrophied muscle of collective sensitivity,” wrote the great art critic Achille Bonito Oliva.

12
Gallery
Exhibition Artist
Anyanwu · PYRAMID
Hand-painted 3D print sculpture
12×12×12 in

Anyanwu is the artistic practice of Nigerian artist, filmmaker, and world-builder Somto Ajuluchukwu.

At the heart of Anyanwu’s work is a central question: what might Africa’s societies, symbols, institutions, and systems of power have become if their evolution had not been interrupted by colonialism? His practice does not approach the past as nostalgia, but as a living source of possibility — a foundation from which new futures can be imagined, designed, and built.

For OURS, Anyanwu presents the Education sculpture from Systems of Power, a body of work that reimagines nation-building through six interdependent pillars: Housing, Health, Education, Environment, Infrastructure, and Economy. Each sculpture is conceived as both an architectural object and a philosophical symbol, asking how societies survive, evolve, and serve the people within them.

The Education sculpture reflects knowledge as one of the most vital infrastructures of any civilization. Drawing from the form of the pyramid as a symbol of ascent, accumulation, and structured wisdom, the work imagines education not simply as schooling, but as a system of memory, imagination, cultural continuity, and collective empowerment.

Through the Systems of Power game, Anyanwu invites players to see Africa not only as a place of history, but as a place of unfinished futures that can still be reclaimed, redesigned, and made ours.

14
Gallery
Vanessa Rosa · Little Martian, the Dreamer
Ceramic and glass · 2×2×3 in
Little Martian, the Dreamer (2021) is Vanessa Rosa’s first experiment fusing melted glass with ceramic; the head appears to be liquefying, caught mid-transformation. In the Little Martians universe, heads are seeds: rather than launching spaceships of humans, life spreads through ceramic exoskeletons that draw on whatever local energy they find and carry Earth’s biological and cultural inheritance with them. Dreamer has not yet germinated; it still waits for a host, someone invited to co-create the universe it belongs to.
Vanessa Rosa is a US-based Brazilian visual artist whose work merges physical and digital media into a single storytelling continuum. She creates fictional tales where world history and possible futures intertwine.
“I envision the future with my hands. … They come from an organic Mars, where Earth’s life has evolved so far beyond what we are now that we would struggle to recognize it as our descendant, even though it carries everything we were.”
16
OURS Salon & Exhibition 2026
Sev Gedra · O Quam Cito
Woven garment made of linen and amber
O Quam Cito is a life-sized figure wrapped in inherited household linen encrusted in woven amber that cascades from the face and pools at the feet. The linen is the most intimate material I could find: domestic, inherited, private.
The figure is faceless because legends have no single author. These stories are woven, strand by strand, hand to hand, each retelling adding something, the origin receding. To think about the future is to think about what survives us. The amber carries what we valued. The gaps in the weave hold space for future generations.

Gallery
Giorgia Lupi · 02 Blue
Gouache, acrylic, ink & threads on paper · 14×18 in
Blue is part of a series called Modelli Circolari, and they stem from my obsession with the things I am eager to understand or fascinated by. Each piece has an inner focus circle that hosts symbols, connections, diagrams and words.

02 Blue maps the hidden structure of personal identity and its evolution: how a self is built, layered, and revised over time. What I cannot yet express in language I can lay down on paper and keep looking at.
18
OURS Salon & Exhibition 2026
Ellynne Dec · the illusion of control
Woven glass beads · 12×12×0.5 in
The source pattern for Illusion of Control is discovered as it is generated. It evolves row by row through the simple comparative logic at the heart of XOR: a continual assessment of same and different. No pictorial motif is drawn in advance; the program specifies only a sequence of local operations. Through repetition, material translation, and human error, these operations produce branching structures, nested scales, and symmetries that emerge, drift, fail, and go on to form their own new logic.

The artist translates each computational act into woven glass beads, one cell at a time. The work treats computation as a material procedure. The title names the gap between the precision with which an algorithm can specify its rules and the computational irreducibility that prevents the resulting form from being fully known in advance except by carrying the process through. Ultimately, computation is necessary to advance the frontier of what can be discovered by humans or their agents.

Gallery
Sue Ellen Zhang · The Hummingbird
Oil on canvas · 30×40 in
The Hummingbird draws from the Futurist movement's fascination with speed, motion, and technological progress. I wanted to translate that sense of energy through softer, organic forms inspired by the natural world.

The painting imagines a future in which technology and nature are not opposing forces, but systems capable of evolving together. Its movement suggests both possibility and the responsibility to shape progress with care.

OURS Salon & Exhibition 2026
Seungjun Na · Paradise of Rumors
Digital collage · 36×48 in
Commissioned by Medici Magazine for OURS
This piece is meant to evoke the feeling of discovering another small world hidden within a secluded pond surrounded by lush plants. On a lotus leaf floating in the pond, there is a miniature world where children are building structures made of LEGO bricks, representing technology built upon art and science. The lotus leaf also has a sail. It symbolizes the hope that everyone on it is moving together toward the same destination with a shared purpose. “I chose children as the main characters because I believe that people who still retain a childlike sense of curiosity and innocence are often the ones capable of imagining groundbreaking changes and truly original ideas. I look forward to a future where such ideas open the door to entirely new worlds.”

Denis Pakowacz · Magnetobiology
Series · penwork & digital · 6×8 in
Commissioned by Leverage for OURS

Denis Pakowacz makes highly detailed work inspired by dark art, sci-fi, fantasy, and mythology, favoring ink graphics with intricate detail and clean linework — a medium for illustrations that tell a story.

Here that storytelling turns to magnetobiology: how magnetic fields, even ones as weak as the Earth’s, act on living things. Science has not yet agreed on how life uses them, and that open question is the reason this series exists.

Combining an ever-growing understanding of grounded scientific work with speculative imagination, Olli Payne aims to build culture and expand popular knowledge around cutting-edge scientific fields and how they may shape a better future for humanity.
Materia Alchemical was inspired by the Nucleonics Institute's hunt for radiation-free energy. The piece presents an imperfect lattice wherein rigid and colorless structure bends, allowing for the brilliant emergence of new and energetic color.

Dylan Weiler · Possibilia
Oil on canvas · 24×36 in
100% of proceeds support the Foundation for Future Aesthetics
In this vision, two hikers and their robot companion pause their trek to take in the view of their city, a world where humanity and technology are balanced and thriving. Painted in oil by Dylan Evans Weiler, Possibilia became the cover of Issue 0 of the Foundation's science-fiction magazine, a home for optimistic, realistic visions of the future. for Artists
by Mauricio Pommella
1
CREATE
Your work begins with you.
2
OWN
The artist should own more than the act of creation.
3
RECORD
Every artwork has a history. Make it visible.
4
PROVE
Provenance should be verifiable, not just trusted.
5
CONNECT
Build relationships that outlive platforms.
6
PARTICIPATE
Do not just use systems. Help shape them.
7
QUESTION
Technology is not automatically freedom. Ask who holds the power.
8
COLLABORATE
The future is built through communities, not gatekeepers.
9
LEARN
Knowledge is the foundation of decentralization.
10
BUILD
Do not wait for permission to create the future.
The artist is not just a creator, but the owner of the record, the builder of the system, and the teacher of the future.

Mauricio Pommella
The Pope
Video illustration
On-chain
Edition 1/1
The Teacher archetype: a leader, innovator, and mentor who stands for both spiritual and technological revolution. He is determined to bring consensus, peace, and positive change to the world through blockchain and distributed-ledger technologies — an optimist and a motivating force, passionate about the benefits they can bring.
The Pope inspires and empowers the global crypto community through knowledge and guidance, a role model who champions a better future built on innovation. He uses his wisdom to mentor others and to encourage trust and collaboration, believing in the power of decentralized organizations and consensus. Above all he is an evangelist of change and progress — a catalyst in the merging of traditional systems and values with the disruption of the crypto world.

Ledgerworks
Recycle Group · Forest of Expired Links
Video / experiential
On-chain
Edition 1/1
Display included
The installation is an artificial forest landscape. Expired links are depicted on each leaf and in each fragment of the landscape, a reference to sources of information that have disappeared. The video loop walks through an endless forest in which the source of information is lost, raising the question of the fragility of knowledge in the modern world.
Nothing here is digitally rendered. The forest was physically built from recycled plastic film, LED, and plywood, then filmed. The work continues Recycle Group’s exploration of the materialisation of the virtual traces of humanity, and belongs to their New Nature project.

OURS Salon & Exhibition 2026
AnjolaDave · An Ending, A Beginning
3D digital
On-chain
Edition 1/1
Display included
Everything is a cycle; life itself is consistently in a flux, taking different states, ups and downs, rises and falls, light and dark, peace and chaos. But most of all beginnings and endings. I feel like this is the part that gives life true meaning. Knowing that at some point everything ends to give room to a new beginning, which then gives room to a new ending. To know each fleeting moment of beauty isn’t guaranteed makes it all the more special.
Knowing how far we’ve come to reach this point as a people from different backgrounds now interconnected by the boundless nature of technology, I believe there are no limits to how high we’re going to go.

Yura Miron · Solara Plaza
Digital illustration
On-chain
Edition 1/1
Display included
‘Solara Plaza’ from the ‘Solara Nexus City’ series unveils a future where architecture breathes and lives in harmony with both nature and the cosmos. Towering structures of shimmering solar panels and glass orbs rise like celestial bodies, capturing the sun’s energy while reflecting the vibrancy of the earth below. Intricate, organic arches stretch above the plaza, resembling the limbs of ancient trees. These forms shelter communal spaces where people gather, converse, and share ideas for a harmonious world.
In this utopian reality, human innovation is grounded in principles of sustainability and compassion. Solara Plaza offers a vision of a future where technology and spirituality converge, where energy flows freely, and where every step taken is toward a brighter, greener tomorrow.

OURS Salon & Exhibition 2026
Nahuel Aquiles · Self-Similar
Biodata-guided pattern generation
On-chain
Personalized 1/1
GenPi is a small project run by scientist and artist Nahuel Aquiles. Biologically generated digital works are a way for our bodies themselves to take on and express artistic form, using either DNA reports (Ancestry.com, 23andMe) or biological time-series data (Oura, Apple Health).
Self-Similar serves as real example. The essential input from biodata is a timestamped trace of living time: rhythms, intervals, changes, gaps, accelerations, recoveries, and irregularities. The output is an abstract science-art transduction: a reproducible visual form emerging from mathematical transformations of biological information.
Create yours at genpi.org
GenPi donates a portion of proceeds to the Foundation for Future Aesthetics.

Collecting On-Chain
See something you love? Collecting it is simpler than it sounds. Most of the work on this wall is sold in US dollars, just like a traditional gallery, and your print comes home with you tonight. (The Pope is the one exception, sold in ETH.)
Each work also lives on-chain as an NFT: a permanent, public record of the piece and who owns it. To receive yours, all you need is a free crypto wallet.

New to web3? Don’t worry about a thing tonight: buy what you love, take your print home, and we’ll handle the on-chain side with you.

We support on-chain works and the artist’s choice to embrace this ledger in order to maintain sovereignty and give their works permanence, livelihood, and a public record of its creation and its journey.

Ugly and Unwarranted

A Possibilia story
Ugly and Unwarranted
by Christian Wolff
37
Ugly and Unwarranted

Late autumn, 2043. It’s early evening and the Jules family has gathered around the dinner table to listen to the judicial commentary livestream and cast their votes.

“Kids!” called Maddy Jules. “Dinner is on!”

A few seconds passed with no answer. “Oh,” she sighed. “Rumba, go find them.”

The family’s multi-purpose sweeper bot turned on and rolled towards the stairs. “Finding children,” it said, in its soft robotic voice.

Jake, Maddy’s husband, came up from behind and held her. She closed her eyes and relaxed into him, glad for the short moment they had together before dinner and voting.

After a moment, Jake spoke. “I have to fly out again,” he said.

“When?” said Maddy, still enjoying the embrace.

“Tomorrow morning. They’re converting another data center in Houston. I have to be there.”

“Why don’t they just give it to the citizens?” said Maddy, pulling away for a moment to touch the tablet on the wall. “Rumba, where are they?”

38
Possibilia Magazine

“The ‘citizens’?” said Jake, shaking his head. “Houston doesn’t do that sort of thing.”

Suddenly there was a crash and a loud tumble as their two children, Nev and Harlan, came running down the steps.

“What’s for dinner?” said Nev, smiling like a little goon. One of his front teeth was missing.

“Please don’t send Rumba for us, mom,” said Harlan, trailing after. “Use our phones.”

Rumba came bobbling down the stairs. “Children acquired,” it said.

“We’re not ‘acquired,’” Harlan said. “We’re not property.”

“Let’s eat,” said Jake. “Your mother has prepared us an entire homemade meal this evening.”

“Ooh,” said Harlan, brightening up.

“And we have voting,” said Maddy.

“Right,” said Harlan. “I’ll get my hard wallet.”

“No, we’ll get them after we eat,” said Jake. “Let’s turn on the stream. We want everyone here to be well-informed when they cast their vote. Isn’t that right, Nev?”

“Yes,” said Nev, climbing into his chair.

39
Ugly and Unwarranted

Nev was six. Harlan was thirteen. Both were old enough to vote on matters of public aesthetics.

Maddy and Jake served the meal, chicken with herbs and lentils with butternut squash, warmed and garnished with chives and Icelandic skyr.

“Luteal,” said Jake, smiling at Maddy.

“And autumnal,” said Maddy, smiling back.

“This is great!” said Nev, picking up his fork. The family had still not gotten prepared meals to work. The superiority of home-cooked dinners was a point of solid consensus.

“Is everyone ready?” said Jake, reaching for the kitchen sound system control…
